snapshot.title: TNPSC Geography: Indian Rivers & Climate
snapshot.exam_hook: 🎯 TNPSC Geography Hook: Godavari: Dakshin Ganga. Narmada/Tapti: West flow. SW Monsoon: 75% India rain. Tsangpo: Brahmaputra. Mawsynram: Wettest.

quick_notes.title: Himalayan Rivers
quick_notes.detail: Perennial (flow year-round). 1. Indus (origin: Mansarovar). 2. Ganga (formed by Alaknanda & Bhagirathi). 3. Brahmaputra (Tsangpo in Tibet).
quick_notes.explanation: Himalayan rivers are called perennial, which means they flow with water all year round, even in the dry season, because they are fed by melting snow and glaciers. The Indus River begins near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet. The Ganga River is formed when two smaller rivers, the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi, join together in the Himalayas. The Brahmaputra River is known as the Tsangpo while it flows through Tibet before entering India. These three rivers are the major river systems that originate in the Himalayan mountain range.

quick_notes.title: Peninsular Rivers
quick_notes.detail: Seasonal (rain-fed). East-flowing (into Bay of Bengal): Godavari (Dakshin Ganga - longest in South), Krishna, Cauvery. West-flowing (into Arabian Sea): Narmada, Tapti (flow through rift valleys).
quick_notes.explanation: Peninsular Rivers are rivers that flow through the southern part of India, and they are called seasonal because they depend entirely on rain for their water, meaning they dry up in the dry season. These rivers are divided into two groups based on where they empty: the east-flowing rivers, which go into the Bay of Bengal, include the Godavari, Krishna, and Cauvery, while the west-flowing rivers, which go into the Arabian Sea, include the Narmada and Tapti. The Godavari is the longest river in South India and is called the Dakshin Ganga, which means the Ganga of the South. The Narmada and Tapti are special because they flow through rift valleys, which are long, narrow cracks in the Earth's crust created by the land splitting apart, instead of flowing on flat ground like most other rivers.

quick_notes.title: Indian Climate (Monsoon)
quick_notes.detail: 4 Seasons: Winter (Jan-Feb), Summer (March-May), SW Monsoon (June-Sep), NE Monsoon (Oct-Dec). SW Monsoon provides 75% of India's rain.
quick_notes.explanation: The Indian climate has four seasons. The first season is Winter, which lasts from January to February. The second is Summer, from March to May. The next is the South-West Monsoon season, often called SW Monsoon, from June to September. The word monsoon means a seasonal wind that brings rain. The SW Monsoon gives India about 75 percent of its total rainfall for the year. The last season is the North-East Monsoon, or NE Monsoon, from October to December.

quick_notes.title: Jet Streams & Western Disturbances
quick_notes.detail: Jet streams influence the arrival of monsoons. Western Disturbances bring winter rain to North India (beneficial for Wheat).
quick_notes.explanation: Jet streams are very fast, narrow bands of strong wind that blow high up in the atmosphere, around 9 to 16 kilometers above the ground. These winds help push weather systems, like the monsoon rain clouds, from one place to another, so they influence when the summer monsoon arrives over India. A Western Disturbance is a specific type of storm that comes from the west, starting over the Mediterranean Sea, and it brings winter rain to the northern parts of India, especially in states like Punjab and Haryana. This winter rain is very useful for the wheat crop because it provides moisture during the growing season, helping the wheat plants develop before the hot summer harvest.

quick_notes.title: Climatic Facts
quick_notes.detail: Mawsynram (Meghalaya) is the wettest place in the world. Thar Desert is the driest. "Mango Showers" (Kerala/Karnataka) help in ripening mangoes.
quick_notes.explanation: Mawsynram, a town in Meghalaya state in northeastern India, receives the highest average annual rainfall on Earth, making it the wettest place in the world. In contrast, the Thar Desert, located in the northwestern part of India, receives very little rain and is considered the driest region in the country. "Mango Showers" is the local name for pre-monsoon rain showers that occur in the states of Kerala and Karnataka, usually in April and May. These light rain showers help mangoes grow and ripen just before the main rainy season begins. The term "pre-monsoon" means the period just before the monsoon season, which is the season of heavy rain that typically starts in June.

lesson_intro: Today we master the 'Hydrology and Weather' of India. We study the contrast between the perennial Himalayan rivers (Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra) and the seasonal Peninsular rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery). We also explore the 'Monsoon'—the pulse of India—and why it rains differently in different regions. For TNPSC, knowing the 'West-flowing' rivers (Narmada, Tapti) and the characteristics of the Southwest Monsoon is vital.
